doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Awakening, spirituality and teacher Tad Shetler
summary: Six months back in the Air Force he has a spiritual awakening, discards his jazz records and studies Simandl with Tad Shetler.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: you know what I mean? Anyway, I went back in the Air Force and I did this thing, and within six months I had an awakening. I mean really. I hit a low one day and then I had to go through these changes. I don’t know, it’s mental, physical, and it’s like an awareness came over me. I began to investigate spirituality a little bit. Psychology. All the books that I could read on the subjects that were on the base library I began to investigate. And I got rid of all my jazz records. And I had a whole slew of, I just tossed all of that aside. And while this was happening, going through this change, one of the guys came into the barracks one day and says, “John,” he says, “I found you a bass teacher.” As if like, you know, he just came out of nowhere. The guy used to play with the Cleveland Orchestra. His name was Tad Shetler. He played with them for about, well quite a number of years, over ten years, had to be. And he was also a pianist, a concert pianist. And after we got to meet each other I found out that he couldn’t get a job playing concert piano so he went to bass. And he had studied with the premier, the first chair of Boston. So in a sense I had gotten my teacher indirectly through him. And Mr. Shetler, I stayed with him for a couple of years, two or three years and learned what I could. Talk about — an awful sound I got out of the instrument, it was terrible. That Kay bass, it was terrible. Scratchy — didn’t know anything about bows or anything. And he taught me out of the Simandl Book, Franz Simandl. That’s the so-called bass Bible. And we worked with that and I scratched my way through it for about two or three years. And then somebody came up to me and said, “John, you want to go overseas? There’s an opening in Iceland.”
